chunks.title: About
chunks.text:
Andrian Than — software engineer building LLM agents for real users.

I'm a computer science student at San Jose State (3.7 GPA, graduating Spring 2027) who builds LLM agents for real users: copilots grounded in data, tested against golden sets, and shipped with the infrastructure to keep them honest.

I've also mentored 30+ people on working with AI coding tools like Cursor and Claude Code, including how to review and verify AI-generated changes.

Outside of engineering I lead in Alpha Kappa Psi and Spartan Analytics.

chunks.title: Alpha Kappa Psi – Omega Phi
chunks.text: Built two internal tools nobody asked for, after seeing the manual work: a membership intake pipeline that runs an application from the first email to a booked interview, and an opportunity bot that posts job listings to a Discord channel. The intake work saves 21+ hours of manual work, and 50+ members use the listings bot to apply.

chunks.title: Alpha Kappa Psi – Omega Phi
chunks.text:
The pipeline takes a membership application from the first email to a booked interview, with no manual step in between.
Problem

The VP Membership ran membership intake by hand: read the email, answer the applicant's questions, check the attachments, file everything, and go back and forth to find a time that worked. It was the same sequence for every applicant, done by one person.
What I built

A pipeline that watches the intake mailbox and runs that sequence. It classifies each incoming email, answers the applicant's question from a knowledge base, validates the attachments, files everything in Drive, and reads the applicant's availability to propose interview slots. When a question is not in the knowledge base, it flags the email for a person instead of guessing.
How it is used

It was built for the VP Membership, who had been doing intake by hand. It saves 21+ hours of manual work, with an 80% improvement in operational efficiency.

chunks.title: Alpha Kappa Psi – Omega Phi
chunks.text:
The bot posts job and internship listings to a Discord channel the members already use.
Problem

Members were each finding listings on their own, so the ones who did not ask around missed the ones posted elsewhere.
What I built

A scraper that collects listings from many sources, including individual company career sites and GitHub, and posts them to the channel. It runs daily and filters listings by role.
How it is used

50+ members use it to apply.

chunks.title: Blue Dome Technologies
chunks.text:
A chatbot I built that answers analysts' labeling questions from the written guidelines, using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with vector embeddings.
Problem

Analysts hit edge cases the guide doesn't make obvious, such as a partly hidden sign or a faded marking, and had to dig through a long document or ask a lead. That slows reviews and leads to inconsistent calls. Interview studies of annotation teams name ambiguous guidelines and edge cases among the main causes of inconsistent labels.
What it does

An analyst asks an edge-case question ("does a partially hidden sign still count?") and gets an answer grounded in the guideline text, with the source clause.
Architecture

A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline in two parts.

 
 
 
 INDEXING (AHEAD OF TIME) ANSWERING (PER QUESTION) 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Guidelines documents (S3) 
 Chunker clauses, sections 
 Embedding model text to vectors 
 Vector store chunks + metadata 
 Analyst question in the review tool 
 Embed + retrieve top matching chunks 
 LLM answers from chunks 
 Answer cites the clause 
 no relevant chunk found: say so, flag the gap for a guideline update 
 
 
 Guideline chatbot architecture 
Indexing, ahead of time: guideline documents are split into chunks, embedded as vectors and stored with their clause ids.
Answering, per question: the question is embedded, the closest chunks are retrieved, and the model writes an answer from only those chunks and cites the clause.
No match: when nothing relevant is retrieved, the chatbot says so instead of guessing, and the gap can be flagged for a guideline update.
Impact
Questions answered per week: about 60
Answers with a cited clause: about 9 in 10
Accuracy on a hand-checked test set: about 85%
"Ask a lead" interruptions: about 15 a week before, about 5 after
Answer time: about 3 seconds

These figures are estimates, not measured results.
About the demo

The window above is a stand-in that runs in your browser: a made-up guide, keyword plus local LSA vector retrieval, and templated answers that quote and cite the matching clause. It shows the shape of the feature, not the production system.

chunks.title: Blue Dome Technologies
chunks.text:
A search tool over the labeled road-scene images that finds images by description, finds images similar to one you pick, and flags near-duplicates, using CLIP-style image and text embeddings.
Problem

Finding more examples of an edge case meant paging through image folders, and repeated scenes got reviewed more than once, which wasted analyst time and skewed the training data.
What it does
Search by text: type a description like "faded lane marking at night" and get matching road scenes.
Similar images: pick an image and see its nearest neighbors, to find more examples of an edge case.
Near-duplicates: flag images that are almost identical, so analysts don't review the same scene twice and training data isn't skewed.
Architecture

Every image is turned into a vector once, and all three features read from the same index.

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Images files in S3 
 Image encoder image to vector 
 Vector index vectors + metadata 
 Text query a scene in words 
 Text encoder same space as images 
 Ranked images closest by meaning 
 Picked image an analyst clicks one 
 Look up its vector already indexed 
 Nearest neighbors more of the edge case 
 Scheduled job checks the whole set 
 Read all vectors compare close pairs 
 Duplicate groups flagged for review 
 
 
 Image search architecture 
Indexing: an image encoder turns each image in S3 into a vector, stored in a vector index with the image's metadata.
Search by text: a text encoder maps the query into the same space as the images, and the closest images are ranked.
Similar images: a picked image's stored vector finds its nearest neighbors.
Duplicates: a scheduled job compares vectors and groups images above a similarity threshold, so analysts review one image per group.
Impact
Time to find examples of an edge case: about 20 minutes before, about 1 minute after
Search quality on test queries: about 8 in 10 of the top 5 results relevant
Images in the index: about 25,000
Near-duplicates found: about 1,800, roughly 7% of the set
Repeat review avoided: about 8 hours (1,800 images at about 15 seconds each)

These figures are estimates, not measured results.
About the demo

The window above is a stand-in that runs in your browser: a made-up set of 27 scenes and a small hand-built attribute space instead of CLIP. Search, nearest neighbors and the duplicate threshold are real logic over that space. It shows the shape of the feature, not the production system.

chunks.title: Blue Dome Technologies
chunks.text:
A human-in-the-loop tool for QA analysts who verify AI-labeled roadway-infrastructure images. I wrote the design spec and built the prototype and the production-ready version.
Problem

The QA analysts who checked AI-labeled roadway images were already using an early prototype of the tool. They found it slow and hard to use. Likely causes: too many clicks per image, no keyboard shortcuts, no clear progress or undo.
Design spec

I wrote the design spec for the production version, then built it.
Architecture

As shipped. A Python Flask backend, a JavaScript frontend and a SQLite database for metadata, with images stored in S3. Analysts review each AI-labeled image and validate it, and TPM 2.0-backed authentication ties a login to a trusted device.

Target architecture. The same Flask API and frontend, with a managed Postgres in place of SQLite.

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Browser JS review UI 
 Flask API TPM 2.0 device auth 
 Postgres labels, verdicts, users 
 S3 bucket image files 
 presigned upload (direct) 
 
 
 Target architecture 
The browser uploads images straight to S3 through presigned URLs, so large files never pass through Flask.
Flask records each image's S3 key, plus AI labels and analyst verdicts, in Postgres.
Device-trust authentication stays at the API.
Key decisions
Device trust: authentication is backed by TPM 2.0, so a login is tied to a trusted device.
Built across a 3-sprint roadmap with a product manager and a UI/UX designer, tracked in Trello, with updates to the founders.
Backend and data
Images live as files in an S3 bucket. The database holds each image's S3 key, and the viewer loads images by signed URL.
Metadata (images, AI labels, verdicts, users) lives in the database.
Why Postgres in the target: SQLite allows one writer at a time, and many analysts saving verdicts at once is its weakest case. Postgres adds concurrent writes, managed backups and filtered queries across labels, reviewers and status.
Impact
Time to review one image: about 45 seconds before, about 15 seconds after
Clicks per image: about 6 before, about 2 after
Analysts using it: about 8
Images reviewed per week: about 1,500
Delivered in: 3 sprints, with a product manager and a UI/UX designer

These figures are estimates, not measured results.

chunks.title: Hanna Center
chunks.text: Built in-house LLM tools with non-technical staff, including a grant-research agent that replaced an enterprise platform, avoiding $30k+ in vendor and subscription cost. Wrote the validation framework for agent accuracy, consistency, and safety.

chunks.title: Hanna Center
chunks.text:
An AI assistant that helps licensed clinicians write progress notes, and check notes they already wrote, against one behavioral-health payer's documentation standards. It expands a clinician's keywords into a note ready for the record, explains every decision, and rates notes pasted in.
Problem

Progress notes fail payer audits or supervisor review when they leave out the elements that show a session was medically necessary. Clinicians needed help writing notes that pass, and a way to learn what a strong note contains without a supervisor reading every one.
What it does
Start a new note: the clinician pastes keywords. The GPT lists everything that is missing in one message, then writes the note and an Expansion Breakdown that explains where each sentence came from and why.
Check a note: the clinician pastes an existing note in any format. The GPT rates it Tier 1, 2 or 3 and says exactly what to fix. It evaluates the note and does not rewrite it.
Stays honest: it never invents symptoms, diagnoses or client responses, and it never softens risk documentation.
Architecture

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Clinician new note, or check one 
 AI assistant instructions + rules 
 Output tier, note, breakdown 
 Knowledge base layered by authority: rules, guidance, guides, lookups 
 file search 
 
 
 Case note chatbot architecture 
One assistant with no backend code of its own. A single instructions file is the source of truth for the rules, the routing table and the output format.
The knowledge base is layered by authority: payer rules first, then audit guidance, sufficiency logic, supporting guides, and structured code and term lookups. When two layers disagree, the higher one wins.
The flow runs input, service type, a check of each of the three note sections, one message listing every gap, then the note and its breakdown.
Key decisions
No embellishment. Every sentence must trace to what the clinician said, because the note is a legal record. Gaps are flagged, not filled.
An authority hierarchy, so payer rules override generic advice.
Three tiers, with hard fails and soft suggestions kept apart. Missing administrative details are never graded.
Risk documentation in three proportional categories, not always required in full.
Telehealth checks are reminders only and never block a note.
A high-capability reasoning model is required, because smaller models loosen the ratings.
Impact
Rating: 3 tiers and 8 hard-fail conditions
Knowledge base: 15 files, including structured lookups of 259 diagnosis codes and 114 intervention terms
Rebuild: 15 to 20 minutes, with the smoke tests re-run after every instruction change

Estimated outcomes:
Time to write a progress note: about 15 minutes before, about 6 minutes after
Clinicians using it: about 12
Notes checked per week: about 50

These figures are estimates, not measured results.
About the demo

The window above is a stand-in that runs in your browser. The real tool is an AI assistant configured with instructions and a knowledge base. The demo uses made-up documentation standards, rule checks for the eight conditions (two of them keyword heuristics), local retrieval for questions, and a note builder where every sentence comes from the input. It is not a language model, and it holds no real clinical content.

chunks.title: Hanna Center
chunks.text:
An agent that finds, scores and tracks grant opportunities for the organization, and replaced an enterprise grant platform. It scrapes funder sources every day, scores each new grant against criteria that staff edit, logs the good ones to a shared sheet, and emails a daily and a weekly digest.
Problem

Finding grants meant searching many funder websites by hand, and the paid platform that did it for us was expensive. The goal was a tool the team owned, that surfaced only grants worth a person's time, and whose scoring non-technical staff could change themselves.
What it does
Scrapes the funder sources every morning and removes duplicates.
Scores each new grant on a seven-flag framework, with a reason for every flag.
Logs grants above the sheet cutoff to a shared tracker where staff approve or skip them.
Emails a daily list of grants above the email cutoff, and a digest on Fridays.
Lets staff retune the scoring in plain English through a custom GPT, with a preview before any change.
Architecture

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Scheduler daily at 6 AM 
 Workflow fans out 
 Scrapers one per source 
 Processing filter, dedupe 
 Vector DB grants + vectors 
 Criteria doc editable by staff 
 Evaluator pre-filter, then score 
 Sheet + email tracker, daily, weekly 
 Editor preview, apply, undo 
 Custom GPT plain English 
 Staff non-technical 
 
 
 Grants agent architecture 
A scheduler starts the day's run. A workflow fans out to one scraper per source, and a processing step filters off-mission items, extracts details with an LLM, embeds them and writes them to a database with vector search.
The evaluator retrieves candidate grants by vector similarity, runs a cheap pre-filter model, then a stronger model scores the survivors against the criteria document.
Scores go to the sheet and the emails. The criteria live in a document that staff can edit, directly or through the custom GPT.
Key decisions
Criteria in a document, so non-technical staff change the scoring without code.
Preview, apply, undo for every edit made through the GPT: a change is previewed, applied with a one-time token that expires, and recorded so it can be reversed.
A cheap model first, a stronger model second, so most grants never reach the expensive step.
Server-side validation of every edit: whitelisted settings and checked values.
A managed scraping service instead of a headless browser, to keep the deployment light.
Impact
Vendor cost avoided: $30k+ across this tool and the incident tool below, replacing an enterprise grant platform and a paid add-on
Sources covered: 39, scraped every day at 6 AM and scored at 9 AM
Scoring: 7 flags and 6 department search profiles; the sheet shows grants scoring 5.0 and up, the email 6.0 and up
Running cost: about $16 to $19 a month, of which the LLM is about $2 to $5
Editing: staff change criteria in plain English, with preview and undo

Estimated outcomes:
Time spent finding grants: about 6 hours a week before, about 1 hour a week of review after
Grants a person reviews each week: about 40 before, about 10 after
Junk grants cut from the review pile: about 70%

These figures are estimates, not measured results.
About the demo

The window above is a stand-in that runs in your browser: twelve made-up grants and funders, seven stand-in flags modeled on the shape of the real framework, and a deterministic scorer. The threshold, the digest and the tracker are live, and the Edit criteria tab runs a real preview, apply and undo with an expiring one-time token. Nothing here is real grant data.

chunks.title: Hanna Center
chunks.text:
A Microsoft Teams bot that lets residential-program staff file an incident report without leaving chat. Staff type a short command, fill a guided five-step form, and the bot creates the record in Salesforce for a supervisor to review. It replaced a paid add-on.
Problem

To file an incident report, staff had to log into Salesforce directly, which meant training, access and finding their way around a complex layout. Frontline staff needed a way to report from the tool they already had open.
What it does
Starts from a command typed in Teams, then walks through five short steps.
Fills in what it can: staff, youth and enrollment details come from lookups, so staff don't retype them.
Reviews before sending, with an edit button on every step.
Creates a Draft incident plus one linked record for each youth involved. A supervisor reviews and approves it in Salesforce.
Architecture

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Teams chat /ir and a form 
 Bot service routes messages 
 One function builds the record 
 Salesforce Draft incident 
 replies through the bot service, form state travels inside each card 
 
 
 Incident bot architecture 
Teams talks to a bot service, which calls one serverless function. The function validates the form, builds the incident and the linked youth records, and writes them to Salesforce.
Replies go back to Teams through the bot service. There is no database, queue or session store: the form's state travels inside each card, and nothing lives outside Salesforce.
Key decisions
One function, which keeps the infrastructure and the cost as small as possible.
State in the card, so the bot is stateless and a restart loses nothing.
Draft only: staff can create reports but not approve them, so a supervisor always reviews.
Dependent picklists with a rule that drops an invalid type and sub-type pair before anything is sent.
Adding a form field is a one-file change: the card input, the state key, the payload and the review card.
Impact
Vendor cost avoided: $30k+ across this tool and the grants agent above, which also replaced a paid add-on
Form: 5 steps, and a submit takes 1 to 3 seconds
Running cost: about $1 to $2 a month
Verification: a 54-check smoke test run after every deploy (53 passing, one transient), and 22 documented failure scenarios with fixes

Estimated outcomes:
Time to file an incident report: about 15 minutes in Salesforce directly, about 3 minutes in Teams
Staff using it: about 25
Reports filed per month: about 80

These figures are estimates, not measured results.
About the demo

The window above is a stand-in that runs in your browser: a Teams-style chat, made-up youth and staff, and the same five-step flow. The dependent picklists, the review screen, the Draft record and the supervisor approval run real logic. Nothing here is real incident data.

chunks.title: Micron Technology
chunks.text: Built an LLM copilot that engineers used daily to investigate wafer failure rates, and a gradient boosting risk model that ranks high-risk wafers, on Python and Snowflake pipelines over high-volume manufacturing data.

chunks.title: Micron Technology
chunks.text:
An LLM copilot over high-volume manufacturing data for HBM wafers. Engineers used it every day to investigate wafer failure rates, asking questions like what made a specific wafer fail.
Problem

The manufacturing data for one wafer spans thousands of production steps. Working through it by hand to explain a failure took a lot of manual analysis time.
What I built

Python and Snowflake SQL pipelines that process the manufacturing data, and a workflow built on Microsoft Copilot and Power Automate that connects Snowflake queries to GPT-based reasoning. An engineer asks a question in plain language, the workflow pulls the relevant data from Snowflake, and the model reasons over what comes back.
How it was used

Used daily by 10+ engineers to investigate wafer failure rates, including what made a specific wafer fail. Explaining one failure went from hours by hand to minutes.

chunks.title: Micron Technology
chunks.text:
A risk classification model that ranks wafers, so engineers know which ones to look at first.
Problem

Engineers cannot review every wafer. They needed the high-risk ones to surface first.
What I built

A gradient boosting model trained on wafers that had failed before. Its inputs include Z-score, failure rate and wafer size, plus other factors such as which machines each wafer went through. It scores each wafer, and the highest scores rise to the top of the list.
How I checked it

I back-tested it on earlier failures.
How it was used

The model scored 1,000+ wafers. Engineers used the ranking to decide which wafers to analyze first and to inform yield optimization work.

chunks.title: Tesla
chunks.text: Built Ask SDP, a tool-calling LLM copilot whose answers can't contain invented numbers, and shipped Forecast Lab, with Chronos-2 forecasts 32% better than baseline on backtest. Built the staging-to-prod pipeline behind 200+ staging deploys a week.

chunks.title: Tesla
chunks.text:
Admin is where access and usage are managed: who can see which tabs, which Ask data categories they can query, and how the dashboard is actually being used.
Problem

Access was managed by editing code, and nobody could see who used the dashboard. The sign-in table held one stage user, so the People view showed 1.
Architecture

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Admin not full access 
 Grants person, group 
 Default-deny not enforcing 
 Person sees tabs, Ask data 
 Audit log every change 
 Request log every request 
 Visits 30 min gaps 
 Usage view per person 
 LLM ledger spend per tab 
 Status view per-tab spend 
 
 
 Admin architecture 
 

Access rules and usage both sit in the backend, and the Admin views read them.
Grants. Per-person and per-group grants decide which tabs and Ask data categories a person sees, and admins change them without a code change.
Grants live in the backend instead of in code, so access changes need no deploy.
Admins are separate from full access. Being an admin lets you manage access; it does not grant every tab.
A separate admin role keeps managing access apart from seeing everything.
Safe changes. Every access change is recorded in an audit log, and dry-run and check actions preview a change and show what a person can see before saving.
An audit log and dry runs make every change visible and checked before it lands.
The default-deny gate. Built, not yet enforcing, and switched on by a server flag.
Building the gate before enforcing it means turning it on is a decision, not a deploy.
Usage from the request log. A visit is a run of requests with gaps under 30 minutes. Per person: active days over 30 days, visits over the last week and 30 days, top tab, Ask request count and LLM spend.
The request log shows what people actually did, while sign-ins showed only one user.
An LLM usage ledger. Spend is recorded per tab and shown on the Status view.
A per-tab ledger shows where LLM spend comes from.
Impact
Per-user monitoring: usage is visible per person from production traffic, including active days, visits, top tab, Ask requests and LLM spend. A real user count is now readable and will replace the resume's user-count claim once it is read. No count is stated here, so this is not measured yet.
Group and per-person tab restrictions: admins grant or remove tabs, and choose which Ask data categories each person can use, with no code change.
Accountable changes: every access change is in the audit log, and a dry run previews it before it is saved.
Cost visibility: LLM spend is recorded per tab on the Status view.

chunks.title: Tesla
chunks.text:
Ask SDP is a tool-calling copilot over live consumption data: planners ask a question in plain language, and every number in the answer comes from a tool result, never from the model's imagination. A golden-set eval harness in CI grades every change to it.
Problem

Demand planners were already asking an LLM questions about consumption data, and the answers read well and were sometimes fiction. A confident invented number is worse than no answer: it flows into a planning decision, and nobody can tell afterwards which figures were real. The copilot could also regress silently, since a prompt change that improved tone could quietly loosen grounding, and the team pushed untested code straight to main.
Architecture

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Question plain language 
 Routing floor code, mandatory 
 Tools in parallel 
 LLM writer drafts answers 
 Output rail checks numbers 
 Typed verdict computed in code 
 Answer sourced figures 
 Golden set + fake number 
 CI gates per pull request 
 Staging every branch 
 Main only path 
 Production after merge 
 
 
 Ask SDP architecture 
 

The shape is a pipeline with one mandatory gate, wrapped in a CI pipeline that grades it on every change.
Routing floor first. A code-gated floor sends data questions to a tool before the model can free-form an answer, so a data question cannot reach the model ungated. On the routing evals it takes tool-routing coverage to 35/35 with 0% free-route answers.
A routing floor in code instead of trusting the model means a data question always reaches a tool first.
Parallel tool calls. When a question needs more than one source, the tool calls run at the same time.
Running calls in parallel instead of one after another makes the wait the slowest call, not the sum.
A cache for repeated lookups. Information that was already fetched is served from the cache instead of being queried again.
Caching allows us to prevent repeated requests to the data source.
Optimized queries. The slowest lookups behind the tools were rewritten to run faster.
Some queries pulled far more of the database than the answer needed, so they were rewritten to fetch only the small piece of information required.
Streaming. The answer reaches the planner as it is written, not after it finishes.
Streaming instead of waiting for the whole answer lets the planner start reading right away.
Output rail. The rail extracts every number in a draft answer and checks each one against the tool results in the conversation. A figure with no source is stripped, and the answer ships without it.
Checking in code instead of in the prompt means an invented figure cannot ship.
A restricted Python tool. Numeric questions go to a Python tool that runs in a separate process with restricted builtins, an import allow-list, and CPU and time limits, returning a checked result into the conversation.
A restricted Python tool lets the copilot compute instead of guess. It limits what generated code can do, but it is not a hard jail.
Typed verdict. Every answer ends in a verdict stating what the data supports, as a field the evals can diff, so a conclusion cannot quietly change between runs.
Computing the verdict in code instead of asking the model means the model cannot override it.
Golden set and gates. A pull request runs the golden set through separate routing, metrics and grounding gates, and a negative control with a fabricated number feeds the grounding gate.
A negative control makes the gate fail on purpose every run, so a gate that never fails cannot hide a problem.
Impact
Faster insight: planners and analysts get answers to demand questions much faster, without pulling data from several places first. The time saved per question is not measured here.
Answer speed: mean answer time fell from 39 s to 11 s, and the slowest narrative answer from 196 s to 16 s, through parallel tool calls, caching, query optimization and streaming. Quoted from a PR, not re-measured.
Fewer dead ends: 9 of 9 reproduced dead-ends were fixed, which were 8.3% of 109 real turns mined from use.

chunks.title: Tesla
chunks.text:
Campaigns tracks the parts linked to service campaigns and warns planners when a campaign is winding down, so the forecast stops carrying demand that will not come back.
Problem

Campaign demand inflates a part's history, and when a campaign winds down the forecast keeps expecting it. Most campaign-linked parts carried a positive two-year over-forecast, worth tens of millions of dollars at unit cost. That is the size of the problem, not part of the impact.
Architecture

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Campaign data parts, service 
 Snapshot one, shared 
 Wind-down best of three 
 Actionable alert parts 
 Views four, CSV export 
 Simulator P10/P50/P90 
 Held for verification 
 Weekly email one per planner 
 
 
 Campaigns architecture 
 

The gate, the views and the notices read the same snapshot of campaign-linked parts, so every planner sees the same numbers.
One snapshot. The gate, the views and the notices read the same snapshot of 223 campaign-linked parts across 131 campaigns.
One snapshot instead of each view querying live means every planner sees the same numbers.
The wind-down gate. Pace share of service units over 8, 13 and 26 weeks, best of the three, against the 10% threshold. 54 parts are on the alert list.
The best of three windows instead of a single one keeps a short dip from triggering an alert.
Held for verification. Parts with unexplained bulletin demand or low-confidence complaint demand are held out of the actionable list.
Uncertain parts are held for verification instead of cut, so they are checked and not counted.
Four views. Alerts, all parts, campaigns, and bulletin demand missing from the campaign list, with CSV export and on-hand inventory by warehouse.
The simulator. A completion simulator gives P10/P50/P90 dates, backtested on 94 past campaigns.
A completion range instead of a single date shows how uncertain a campaign's end is.
Per-planner notices. One email per planner with only their parts, a consolidated copy to the team, and one listing bulletin demand missing from the campaign list. 6 planners receive alerts.
One email per planner instead of one for everyone keeps each notice short enough to read.
Dollars as exposure. Forecast dollar figures are forecast exposure, and time-saved dollars use a placeholder rate.
Dollars are exposure, not cash, so the page does not claim savings that are not booked.
Impact

Estimated impact based on a snapshot.
Flagged and actionable: about $13.3M of forecast cut was flagged across the 54 alert parts, and 44 of them are actionable, about $4.9M. The other 10 parts, about $8.4M, are held for verification and not counted.
Expected impact: about $1.2M to $2.5M of excess forecast exposure removed over 26 weeks, which is 25% to 50% of the actionable $4.9M, an estimate.
Backtest evidence: the shipped model was $6.5M to $9.3M closer to actual use than the books across 36 flagged parts and 23 campaigns, not booked.
Time saved: roughly 300 to 350 hours, about $30k to $35k at a placeholder rate of $100 an hour, not an employer rate. It is an estimate across the projects on this page (this includes Forecast Lab's 80-hour estimate), mostly from spike investigations at about 200 hours.

chunks.title: Tesla
chunks.text:
The unified planning dashboard is the React and FastAPI app planners live in, and I shipped it end to end. Overview, Part Summary, Ask, Forecast Lab, Campaigns, the KPI tabs, Home and Admin sit in one app, and the work was making it open fast, stay correct on real data, and stay easy for other people to extend.
Problem

Planning data was scattered across about eight live database sources, around seven of them DuckDB or parquet files. Each source had its own Streamlit dashboard, so answering one question meant clicking through several tools with different layouts and filters. That friction was the problem the unified dashboard exists to solve: one place, one sign-in, one navigation, one data layer. The code had a matching problem. The app had grown screen-first, features reached directly into whatever data they needed so a change in one screen could break another, and adding a tab meant editing the shell.
Architecture

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Browser planner 
 SWR cache gzip, lazy load 
 API reads only 
 Warm registry last good copy 
 Memory cap stops warming 
 Weekly ETL fails loud 
 Backends pooled, DuckDB 
 Startup build single-flight 
 Disk snapshot atomic, shared 
 
 
 Dashboard architecture 
 

The rule behind the design: the request path only reads, and all building happens at startup or in the background. The same information leaves the database once, not once per person or per page view.
A warm registry, built at startup. Each worker holds the last good copy in memory. A request gets that copy, or an instant "warming up" reply while the first build finishes.
Building ahead of time instead of per request keeps users from waiting on several backends.
A "warming up" reply instead of queueing stops waiting requests from piling up and competing with the build.
A shared disk snapshot. A build is written to disk once as an atomic snapshot, every worker loads that file instead of querying the backends, and a restart reads it too.
One shared build instead of one per worker means concurrent requests share one build instead of starting their own.
A browser cache. A stale-while-revalidate cache answers from its own copy and refreshes in the background, so going back to a page asks the server for nothing.
The cache prevents repeated requests to the server when a planner goes back to a page.
Bounded resources. Connections are pooled, DuckDB runs as one shared connection with a memory limit, a semaphore bounds how much warms at once, and a 3500 MB ceiling stops hot-part warming.
Pooling and a ceiling keep memory and connections bounded; hot-part warming stopped at 15 of 25 parts.
A light first load. Gzip is on and charts load only when they are needed.
Sending less up front beats relying on a fast network.
Read-only requests. Only a build touches the databases, and the dashboard's reads are SELECT-only.
Read-only means a bad query can be slow but cannot damage data.
A data path that fails loud. The weekly ETL streams its input, builds are verified before an atomic swap, a loader never deletes the live database before its replacement is verified, and freshness is polled every 10 minutes with gates that stop stale data being served as current.
Failing loud instead of reporting green means stale data no longer goes unnoticed.

A second rule keeps the code modular: the shell owns sign-in, navigation and discovery, and tabs plug into it through a manifest, so new work adds files instead of changing the shell.

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Tab manifest + one UI file 
 Shell auto-discovery 
 Import errors contained 
 Kill switch runtime flag 
 Mounted tab behind sign-in 
 Skipped and reported 
 Backend data 
 Data facade one data client 
 
 
 Modular architecture 
 

 
Manifests and auto-discovery. A tab is a manifest plus one frontend file. The shell finds it, mounts it behind sign-in, and nothing is registered by hand.
Discovery instead of registration means a contributor adds files and never edits the shell.
Kill switch. A runtime flag turns any tab off for everyone without a deploy.
A kill switch lets a broken tab be turned off at once, without a redeploy.
Import isolation. A tab whose import fails is skipped and reported instead of crashing the shell.
Isolated imports mean one broken tab does not take the app down.
Tabs share one process instead of running one each, so a tab that hangs can still affect the others. Per-tab processes are a proposal only.
Reusable components. Screens use a shared button and fetch layer instead of writing their own, and lint rules keep them on it.
Reusing shared building blocks means AI coding tools reuse what already exists instead of regenerating new components each time, so there is less new code to review and less drift between screens.
A data-client facade. Screens reach data through one small facade, and lint guards stop imports past it.
A facade instead of screens reaching into data means a change in one screen cannot break another.
Impact
First cold load: 71 to 100 s before, 6 s after, measured (local).
Six simultaneous cold loads: 112 s before, 4.4 s after, measured (local).
First request after a restart: blocked for 110 to 189 s before; now a "warming up" response in under 250 ms, measured (local).
Back from Part Summary: 12 requests, 6.9 MB and 2.4 s before; no network requests and 0.05 s after, measured (local).
Campaigns load: 22 requests and 8.5 MB before, 9 requests and 0.2 MB after, measured (local).
Entry JavaScript: 5.8 MB before, 1.1 MB raw and 335 KB gzipped after, measured (local).
First paint at 25 Mbps: 2.3 s before, 0.37 s after, measured (local).
On stage: Overview rows load in about 4.6 s and Campaigns in about 1.9 s, measured (stage).
Data restored: about 66M rows back in place, and the association data moved from early May to early July, measured.
Scalability: more people can contribute without stepping on each other. A new tab is a manifest and one frontend file, and a tab that fails to import is skipped instead of breaking the app. The like-part tab, contributed by a teammate, is the first built on the shell from outside.
A smaller shell: the main app file went from 3,141 to 597 lines, so adding a tab no longer means editing a huge file, measured (local) from the repository.
Nothing broke: the route table is byte-identical at 165 routes, measured (local) from the repository.
Cost to watch: stage RAM idles at 1.75 GB and reached 3.6 to 4.0 GB after opening every deep-dive tab on a cold part, against the 3500 MB ceiling, measured (stage). Production runs one worker and is not yet verified.

The figures are a mix of local and stage runs, so treat them as medium confidence.

chunks.title: Tesla
chunks.text:
Forecast Lab is where Chronos-2 forecasts reach planners: a watchlist, shaping controls for business knowledge, and a firming flow that previews a change before it is committed to the firming system.
Problem

Firming a forecast used to mean exporting a CSV, filling in a template and uploading it by hand. Inside the app, batches of 4 or more parts took 50 to 87 s and batches of 6 or more timed out, and the failures were swallowed, so the forecast overlays came back empty with no error. The baseline forecast also missed shape the business could see coming.
Architecture

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Watchlist selected parts 
 Batch request one call 
 Warm runner Chronos-2 loaded 
 Shaping buffer layers 
 Dry-run shows the change 
 Loud failure error, not blank 
 Firming only write path 
 Commit planner confirms 
 
 
 Forecast Lab architecture 
 

Generating a forecast and writing one are separate paths, because a forecast is cheap to regenerate and expensive to undo.
Generate path. A planner submits a batch of parts, which goes to the warm Chronos-2 runner in one call. Each part's forecast is displayed as it finishes while the rest populate in the background.
Chronos-2 was chosen over LightGBM and TimesFM in the team's own backtest, cutting lag-zero error from $17.0M to $11.6M, 32% better than baseline.
A warm runner instead of loading per request removes the start-up cost from every call.
One call per batch instead of one per part avoids paying overhead for each part.
Showing the first result instead of waiting for the batch lets the page paint fast.
The slow batches came from a database query plan that flipped on a 54M-row table, so an index hint fixed it instead of changing the model, with identical forecast output.
Shaping and buffer layers. Planner adjustments sit on top of the generated forecast, recorded as a diff that never changes the model.
Shaping layers let planners add what the data does not know without touching the model.
Write path. Firm Selected computes the change and shows a dry-run preview. Only a commit writes to the firming system, and the app then checks with the production system that the firm went through.
Every firm is a dry run first and is checked with production afterwards, instead of trusting that the write went through.
Failure path. A failed batch returns an error instead of an empty overlay.
Failures used to be swallowed and come back as empty overlays, so they now return an error.
Scope. South America warehouses are part of the same flow, and the backtest switcher is off by default, so planners see the live forecast unless they ask for the backtest.
The live forecast is what planners work from, so the backtest is off unless they ask for it.
Impact
From forecast to production in one place: a planner can now review the production forecast, adjust it and push it live without leaving the tool. That workflow used to mean hopping between several platforms, and updates now reach production far faster. A dry-run preview shows every change before anything is written. The speed-up is not measured here.

chunks.title: Tesla
chunks.text:
Part Summary is the one-stop page for a single part: search for it, and the sub-tabs show its status, consumption, failure rates and breakdowns in one place.
Problem

To understand one part, planners pulled each view from a separate report: consumption from one place, failure rates from another, location and correction-code breakdowns from somewhere else. Investigating a demand spike meant assembling those by hand before any thinking could start.
Architecture

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Part search one part 
 Sub-tab its slice only 
 Slice loader single-flight 
 Pooled SQL reused clients 
 Backend can be slow 
 LLM insights to Overview 
 Sub-tab view chart or matrix 
 Stream in retry on timeout 
 Weekly demand aggregated 
 
 
 Part Summary architecture 
 

Part Summary loads only what the open sub-tab needs, and loads it in a way that survives a slow backend.
Six sub-tabs for one part. Overview (AI-generated insights on current status), consumption over time, failure rates and their trend, a location by build-year matrix, a correction-code matrix, and a breakdown of customer symptoms next to correction codes.
One playbook powers both Ask and the sub-tabs, instead of two separate investigations.
A narrowing path that ends in a verdict replaces a wall of charts, and captions that could mislead were removed.
Slices per sub-tab. Each sub-tab fetches its own slice, so opening Overview does not pay for the matrices.
Fetching a slice per sub-tab instead of one big load means opening Overview does not pay for the matrices.
Single-flight and pooled SQL clients. Two requests for the same slice share one query, and connections are reused instead of opened per request.
Sharing queries and connections prevents repeated work on repeat opens.
Request limiting. Submitting a part sends a burst of requests at once, one for each slice. The number running against the backend at one time is capped, and the rest wait their turn.
Limiting the burst instead of sending every slice at once keeps a single part search from overloading the database.
Weekly demand aggregation. Demand is aggregated to weeks before it reaches the page.
Weekly aggregation instead of raw rows means the page handles far less data.
Stream in, retry on timeout. Results stream in as they arrive, and a slice that times out is retried instead of leaving a blank chart.
Streaming with a retry instead of all-or-nothing means a slow slice does not blank the page.
Impact
Spike investigation time: about 2 hours before, about 25 minutes after, planner-reported. It was reported by planners, not measured, and it is not multiplied by the number of users.
Back-navigation speed: the measured numbers are in the Dashboard section above.

chunks.title: Tesla
chunks.text:
Slideshow generation rebuilds the weekly executive deck inside the app, on top of the weekly ETL that built the data the deck and the KPI files read.
Problem

The executive deck was assembled by hand from queries that drifted between runs, and the KPI files planners needed every Monday were built by hand too. Each cycle cost hours, and a number in the deck could disagree with the number in the app.
Architecture

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Weekly run schedule stopped 
 Build tables week's demand 
 Verify before any read 
 Verified set one source 
 Regenerate in-app button 
 Exec deck PPTX download 
 KPI files accessories 
 Weekly CSV Part Miss by Lag 
 
 
 Slideshow generation architecture 
 

The deck and the KPI files came from one weekly run, so the number in the deck matched the number in the app.
A weekly GitHub Actions run. It pulled the week's demand data and built the tables behind the deck and the accessories KPI numbers.
A schedule makes the CSV appear without anyone asking, and the in-app regenerate covers the rest.
Verified before use. The build was checked before anything read it.
Verifying the build instead of trusting it keeps a bad run from reaching the deck.
One source, several outputs. The 77-slide executive deck, the accessories KPIs and the Part Miss by Lag CSV, published every KPI Monday, all read the same verified tables.
One source instead of separate builds means the deck cannot disagree with the app.
Regenerate in the app. A Regenerate button rebuilds the deck from the current data with a PPTX download, and composer controls stay hidden while they are a work in progress.
Generating the deck instead of assembling it by hand makes it the same every time for the same data.
Unfinished controls stay hidden instead of shipping half-working.
The schedule was later stopped. The scheduled Monday run was later stopped; the in-app regenerate still works on demand.
Impact
Auto-assembled KPI decks: the weekly KPI presentation for cross-functional teams used to be assembled by hand. Weekly demand data now reaches the 77-slide executive deck without a hand-assembled run. The scheduled run saves an estimated 20+ hours per run, an estimate rather than a measured figure.
More in-depth insight: AI is integrated into the deck, and its insights give a qualitative and quantitative overview of specific metrics, areas and zones.
